item.title: Higher education as class commitment
item.description:
In a previous post, I argued that Bryan Caplan’s signaling theory isn’t a good explanation for why college graduates get higher-paying jobs. Instead, I claimed, understanding the role of higher education in the modern West requires sociological explanations. In this post I argue more specifically that getting an undergraduate degree serves as an initiation into a class of cultural elites, variously called the “bourgeois bohemian” (bobo) class, the professional-managerial class (PMC), the “Blue Tribe”, globalists, “symbolic analysts”, or class X. I think of each of these labels as grasping one part of the elephant, but I haven’t yet pinned down a unified description; I’ll mainly use the “PMC” terminology in this post, for reasons I’ll explain in the next section.

Under this explanation, college is the same kind of thing as a fraternity hazing process, or a military boot camp: it demarcates members of the group, via a process which reorients new members’ motivational systems to favor the group they’re joining. College graduates therefore benefit from the nepotism of existing members of their class, which they perpetuate when they gain the ability to make hiring decisions. This lines up well with Bourdieu’s hypothesis that the primary purpose of modern education is to reproduce existing class structures via “consecration” of graduates by academic authorities. However, today’s class dynamics are very different from those of the mid-1900s. The modern PMC is very politically skewed, and implements class nepotism on a visceral emotional level: for example, via deep contempt for populists (e.g. Brexit voters or MAGA supporters); disgust for challenges to modern feminism (e.g. from Scott Aaronson or Robin Hanson); and fear of “falling off” the elite career ladder.

There’s a way in which my hypothesis is just common sense: of course attending Harvard is a path into the American (and indeed global) elite, and of course employers who strongly prefer Harvard students are tracking some kind of status hierarchy. Nor is generalizing from “Harvard graduates” to “all graduates” a very big leap. Unfortunately, no major intellectual traditions have internalized this idea well enough to build on it. Academic sociologists are willing to point at class dynamics everywhere else, but can’t grapple with the ones they themselves are implementing (in part because they’ve abandoned any meaningful standards of rigor).

Other intellectual clusters (like the rationalist cluster I describe here) have developed a kind of “immune response” to vague sociological thinking, and therefore fall back on the closest hypotheses they can formulate in broadly economic language. However, as my previous post argued, this misses a lot. So the main goal of this post is to take a step towards more rigorous sociological explanations of higher education and many other phenomena, by characterizing class dynamics in terms of game-theoretic interactions between rational-ish agents.

I start by drawing on Scott Alexander’s concept of a backscratcher’s club to explain the core benefit of class membership. However, it’s difficult to explain how long-term loyalty to a backscratcher’s club could be incentive-compatible for people who don’t terminally value it. So in the second section, I argue that college serves as a commitment mechanism by changing students’ identities. This is distinct from Caplan’s signaling explanation because signaling is a process of conveying information about existing traits, rather than changing those traits. (Note that I’m specifically avoiding talking about changes in students’ values, because a big part of what it means to be committed to a class is that you’ll defer to the class consensus over your own values. This makes students’ values something of a red herring.)

In the final section, I characterize the resulting class as a “social equilibrium” which is able to propagate and defend itself. (I’ve previously discussed a related concept using the term “distributed agent”, e.g. in this talk, this post, and these slides.) I also give a case study of a (more extreme) historical example of this kind of social equilibrium—namely Chinese foot binding—and its analogies to higher education.

College alumni as a backscratchers club

I’ll start by discussing reciprocal favoritism at smaller scales, before moving on to class-level nepotism. One common-sense benefit of college attendance that I didn’t discuss in my previous post is forming a professional network. This need not be via traditional “networking”—simply making friends is sufficient. A friendship is (amongst other things) a reciprocal arrangement where you expect to favor each other. And the friends you make at university (especially a top university) are likely to be unusually successful.

On an individual level, this can be very advantageous. However, it doesn’t explain why employers so strongly prefer to hire college graduates. When you’re a new grad, your network largely also consists of new grads, who aren’t very helpful to know yet. And while in the longer term having a better network might let you do your job better, it also gives you more opportunities to jump ship to other jobs.

So to explain the college wage premium we need to generalize the concept of reciprocal favoritism. Here I’ll borrow Scott Alexander’s concept of a “backscratchers club”: a group with the rule “club members must favor other club members over outsiders”. (Though this seems like a straightforward concept, I wasn’t able to find any term with the same meaning in the academic sociology literature; pointers welcome.)

Scott notes that an important aspect of such clubs is having some barrier to entry—otherwise everyone could just join it, making favoritism towards other members meaningless. He also argues that such clubs work best when they have plausible “fig leaves” for what the club is about, with favoritism as an implicit norm rather than a legible rule. Being part of a well-functioning backscratchers club should increase your access to desirable jobs, because members of the club will preferentially hire other members (and punish other club members who aren’t nepotistic) in order to remain in good standing within the club.

As a first pass, then, we can explain college attendance as the process of joining a set of overlapping backscratchers clubs. There’s your core friend group; your student groups (including fraternities and sororities); the alumni of your particular university; and finally the group of all university graduates. Picture a hiring manager who sees a resume of someone from the same fraternity or the same university, and puts it at the top of the pile out of a sense of camaraderie or loyalty. My hypothesis is that the wage premium for college students is explained by a similar kind of loyalty amongst college graduates as a whole, plus a sense that they’ll face social punishments for being less nepotistic (e.g. disproportionate blowback if they hire an outsider who performs badly).

I had intended, at this point, to give a more thorough explanation of Bourdieu’s theory of education and class. However, this led me to procrastinate on finishing this post for six months. So for now I’ll focus on a different tradition of class analysis, centered on Barbara and John Ehrenreich’s concept of the professional-managerial class (PMC). This class was originally understood primarily in economic terms—e.g. James Burnham’s The Managerial Revolution offered an alternative to both the capitalist and the Marxist worldviews. However, over time it became more sociopolitically-oriented—in part because “the values of that class completely took over left-liberal political spaces” (as per Catherine Liu, who has written extensively on this new conception of the PMC).

Unfortunately, most of these authors are still working within the PMC’s value system even as they critique the class itself. From a more independent (but still broadly PMC-aligned) perspective, Scott Alexander’s characterization of the “Blue Tribe” does a much better job at capturing the depth of its animus against its class enemies. (I also recommend Sarah Constantin’s concept of “Ra” as a depiction of one closely-related memeplex.) Scott’s Blue Tribe terminology helps to convey that membership isn’t primarily about one’s job title, but rather one’s culture and identity.

There’s some tension between a cultural conception of the PMC, and my characterization of the PMC as being gatekept by formal credentials. I don’t mean to imply that an undergraduate degree is strictly necessary for PMC membership; such illegible coordination at such large scales will always involve somewhat fuzzy boundaries. However, it still seems surprisingly important, in a way which (I’ve argued) can’t be explained by either the standard human capital model or Caplan’s signaling model—for example, undergraduate credentials are often considered even when hiring people with decades of work experience. In the next section I’ll discuss why I think college degrees aren’t just strongly correlated with PMC membership, but are actually playing a load-bearing role in how it operates and propagates.

Initiation rituals as commitment mechanisms

For a backscratcher’s club to remain stable, club members need to reliably follow its rules. However, there are at least two reasons why it’s hard to incentivize them to do so. Firstly, there’s a strong time asymmetry: people primarily benefit from their status as university graduates early in life, but primarily have the ability to favor other graduates later in life. So there’s a clear incentive to accept the favor of other club members when you’re young, but then fail to reciprocate when you’re older—e.g. by hiring the best person for the job rather than another club member.

This might be prevented if club members also punish defectors. However, without any central authority capable of doing so, enforcing group norms is another kind of work that needs to be incentivized somehow. You need people who will punish others for breaking norms, and people who will punish others who don’t punish others for breaking norms, and people who will punish others who don’t punish others who don’t punish others for breaking norms, and… Such equilibria are technically possible—the game theory folk theorems show that a very wide range of equilibria can be stable. But in any realistic setting, a group would fall apart if everyone were only doing the bare minimum they could get away with. (Kevin Simler hypothesises that a “minimum viable superorganism” can avoid this problem, but doesn’t explain how it could avoid internal nepotism.)

So a formal model of backscratchers clubs needs some mechanism by which joining a club actually commits you to following its rules. Credible commitments are in general hard to make, because they require adversarially constraining your future self. I’ll talk about three potential mechanisms for making such commitments—though note that they’re all closely related. The first is simply sunk costs. If you’ve invested a lot of work in climbing one particular social hierarchy, then leaving it to climb another hierarchy becomes less attractive. You may need to find new friends, learn new skills, and incur additional costs to demonstrate your commitment to your new hierarchy.

However, even given these sunk costs, leaving for a healthy faction can easily be more long-term beneficial than staying in an unhealthy faction. For example, I expect that many humanities graduates from the early 2010s would be making more money now (and be happier) if they’d retrained as plumbers after graduating, rather than entering unhealthy white-collar job markets. And sunk costs matter less if other factions will let you rise in them without making additional costly commitments—e.g. the relatively meritocratic hiring policies of Silicon Valley companies make it easier for people in other industries to jump ship.

Another commitment mechanism: requiring people to “burn their bridges” with other factions to rise in their current faction. For example, getting a prominent gang tattoo makes it more difficult to later leave the gang and reintegrate into society. And a politician who viciously attacks another party will tend to have more trouble switching to that party later on. Again, however, this depends on other desirable factions maintaining high barriers to entry, rather than having mechanisms by which former enemies can be forgiven and integrated.

A third way of making credible commitments is by setting up external constraints, like legal contracts. This is difficult to do directly for class membership without that class losing the advantages it gains from illegibility. However, the PMC has managed to weaponize civil rights law to indirectly enforce many constraints that benefit it—e.g. by making it borderline illegal to hire based on IQ tests in America. Overall, legal constraints seem like an important part of the picture, but not the main mechanism by which class loyalty is maintained.

Instead, the main mechanism by which I think college creates class commitment is by rearranging people’s motivational structures, in particular by making their self-esteem dependent on success by the standards of the PMC. This is hard to analyze from an economic perspective; instead, we need to draw on more psychological concepts. In particular, I model most people as being in a constant process of “ego defense”—that is, working to find or maintain internal narratives (like “I’m a well-respected member of my community”, or “I’m a world-class researcher”) which are consistent both with the evidence available to them, and with their sense of social and physical security. A group can induce loyalty in such a person by crowding out their existing narratives in favor of narratives where group membership is a key pillar of their lives. (This seems closely related to what Bourdieu calls “symbolic violence”.)

More concretely, this can happen via putting people through intense experiences which pit their desire to join that group directly against other identities. Narratives in which group membership is crucial (which “predict” compliance with extreme aspects of the initiation ritual) will therefore be reinforced; while other conflicting aspects of one’s identity (like individual dignity) which “predict” noncompliance will be negatively reinforced.

In this post I’ve been using the concept of “identity” in a fairly vague way. Unfortunately, this is because I don’t yet have a clean definition; my best attempt is something like “narratives about themselves that guide agents’ instinctive behavior and conscious deliberation in self-fulfilling ways”. I expect that a better understanding of frameworks like active inference and Garrabrant induction will allow us to pin down this concept much more cleanly (see here and here for two steps in that direction). For now, though, it seems better to think of “identities” in a pre-theoretic way, as the kind of thing we appeal to when trying to describe patriotism, or ego, or Stockholm syndrome.

Intense experiences seem to be particularly effective at shaping identities when they demarcate a sharp boundary between who’s in and who’s out of a club (or between different discrete levels of membership). I’ll call such experiences initiation rituals. The binary nature of initiation rituals makes coordination to enforce norms much easier, because there’s less room for (strategic) ambiguity. This helps explain the sheepskin effect: why graduating from college helps your career much more than dropping out one semester early. With a class as large as the PMC, the boundaries will always be fuzzy nevertheless. But the binary distinction between having a degree or not remains surprisingly relevant for many employers even when hiring people with decades of work experience.

Initiation rituals (especially coming-of-age rituals) are a common feature of pre-modern societies, and are often extremely unpleasant. For example, Scott Alexander summarizes one here:

When an Aboriginal man comes of age, he gets mock-abducted from his parents by unrelated elders and forced to spend five to fifteen years going through a series of grueling initiation rituals. During some parts of the rituals, he must spend months isolated from all other humans, living on his own in the wilderness. During others, he endures horrible mutilations, starting with circumcision and only getting more horrifying and creative from there.

Initiation rituals in modern societies are much less intense, but follow some similar principles. Two of the more obvious examples are hazing processes for fraternities, and military basic camp. Each of these can be very unpleasant by modern standards, typically including a combination of sleep deprivation, physical pain, and social humiliation. Candidates might have many reasons for continuing with this process—e.g. a sense of stubbornness, or concern for their reputation. But regardless, they’ll also be reinforcing the internal narrative that, if they’re willing to put up with this much pain, they must really value joining the group. The process of breaking psychological resistance to group loyalty involves making the initiation ritual painful enough that this narrative is hard to question. Even a long time afterwards, changing your mind involves admitting that you made a very costly mistake—often a psychologically painful process.

Compared with these initiation rituals, college lacks intensity, but makes up for it in length. You typically spent three or four years away from your family and community, surrounded by other young people trying to form their own identities. It’s therefore very easy for those identities to end up anchored to an external status hierarchy—especially for the many students who go into a lot of debt to attend college, and are relying on their newfound class privilege to make that choice financially worthwhile. Dan Wang has a very compelling blog post on the resulting Girardian terror, which I’ll quote at length:

It’s hard to construct a more perfect incubator for mimetic contagion than the American college campus. Most 18-year-olds are not super differentiated from each other. By construction, whatever distinctions any does have are usually earned through brutal, zero-sum competitions. These tournament-type distinctions include: SAT scores at or near perfection; being a top player on a sports team; gaining master status from chess matches; playing first instrument in state orchestra; earning high rankings in Math Olympiad; and so on, culminating in gaining admission to a particular college.

Once people enter college, they get socialized into group environments that usually continue to operate in zero-sum competitive dynamics. These include orchestras and sport teams; fraternities and sororities; and many types of clubs. The biggest source of mimetic pressures are the classes. Everyone starts out by taking the same intro classes; those seeking distinction throw themselves into the hardest classes, or seek tutelage from star professors, and try to earn the highest grades.

There’s very little external intermediation, instead all competitive dynamics are internally mediated. The prizes are so obvious. The big companies that come to career fairs soothingly assure high-status jobs; the speakers at convocation tell us that we too will become as successful as them one day; our peers hold leadership positions at clubs, get internships at exciting companies, and earn those chances to have lunch with the university’s president.

In his blog post School is to Submit, Robin Hanson discusses a related hypothesis: that university attendance became so common because it trained students to submit to hierarchies. However, if university graduates acquired a willingness to submit in general, we’d see more of them submitting to (well-paid) blue-collar work, right-wing politicians, etc. Instead, a version of Hanson’s hypothesis which better fits our observations is that modern universities instill the desire to submit specifically to the PMC hierarchy. One indicator of the strength of this effect is how graduates who come from generational wealth often end up working the same jobs, for the same salaries, as graduates who actually need money. This is very hard to explain in economic terms, but makes perfect sense if those graduates view jobs at McKinsey or Meta (or increasingly OpenAI or Anthropic) as primarily paying them in social status.

Moving beyond individual rationality

So far in this post, I’ve tried to remain reasonably close to the classic “rational individuals” framework. My account of initiation rituals, Dan’s account of Girardian terror, and Robin’s account of submission all describe non-rational mechanisms by which people’s identities change—but they’re still the kind of experience which a rational-ish individual could in principle opt into for the sake of other benefits (e.g. better jobs). I’ve focused on this level of analysis because I think it has the potential to develop into a sociological framework that’s much more rigorous than current academic sociology, as I’ll discuss at the end of this post.

However, while I’m optimistic about the long-term potential of this kind of reasoning, in the short term it can easily miss the forest for the trees. So in this final section of my post I want to zoom out to give a more holistic sense of what’s going on with higher education and the PMC. As one starting point: there’s an important disanalogy between processes like fraternity hazing or basic training and higher education. The former are run by people who want to select and shape initiates to be useful for their institutions. Whereas insofar as college graduation serves as an initiation into the PMC, that happens without any centralized planning or top-down enforcement of class boundaries.

Instead, many people’s individual decisions are steered towards what they think others in their class will support. This kind of distributed coordination can superficially resemble a conspiracy, but actually differs in many ways. In a previous post, I used the term “consensus of power” for the extreme case where individuals’ values don’t matter at all. A more general term, from notable sociologist Talcott Parsons, is “social equilibrium”: a social system which, when disturbed, tends to return to its original state. My understanding (mainly from Fable) is that Parsons didn’t consider social equilibria to be modellable by game theory, precisely because this kind of robustness requires players to internalize shared norms as part of their identities.

Social equilibria are all around us (e.g. tipping culture, or dating culture), but ones with the breadth and influence of the PMC are rare. One that’s somewhat comparable is the Indian caste system, although it’s much more explicit than the PMC. A more implicit (but also very influential) social equilibrium is beauty standards. We typically think of beauty standards as being maintained using relatively little coercion. However, beauty standards linked to class dynamics can motivate extremely costly commitments, like female genital mutilation in Africa or foot-binding in China.[1] I’ll zoom in on the last (and its parallels to higher education) as a case study.

Foot-binding was a horrific practice in which young girls’ feet were compressed hard enough to break bones. After months or years of being bound, their feet permanently deformed to become much smaller and painful to walk on. It also happened a lot: the cultural practice of foot-binding lasted for over a millennium and affected hundreds of millions of women. Wikipedia estimates that “by the 19th century 40–50% of all Chinese women may have had bound feet, rising to almost 100% among upper-class Han Chinese women”.

The nominal purpose of foot-binding was to make girls more beautiful. From our current vantage point, it’s obvious that this was just a fig leaf. One way of systematically identifying fig leaves is asking whether there are much better and cheaper ways of getting the nominal goal. We can also apply this standard to universities: the fact that there are much better and cheaper ways of learning job-relevant skills undermines that explanation for the college wage premium. In turn, though, the fact that there are much better and cheaper ways of signaling desirable traits undermines Caplan’s signaling theory of universities.

Taking the comparison further: husbands who choose to marry women with bound feet are analogous to employers choosing to hire university graduates for much higher salaries than they’d need to pay equally-talented high school graduates. You might object that university students are old enough to rationally opt in to this process, whereas Chinese girls had foot-binding forced on them by their parents. However, the actual reasons why most students go to university seem to have less to do with rational deliberation, and more to do with having already internalized conformist motivations. I like Hazard Spence’s description of primary and secondary school as “lay[ing] the groundwork for stupefaction and domestication” (see also his annotated Open History of American Education).

At this point we’ve moved far enough away from the ideal of individual rationality that I’ll shift to talking about social equilibria as agents in their own right, which are able to propagate and defend themselves using decentralized coordination between their human subagents. One canonical example of this kind of “distributed agent” is Scott Alexander’s ‘toxoplasma of rage’, where he conceptualizes entrenched political conflicts as agents carrying out strategies optimized to reproduce themselves. Compare how the foot-binding process was often carried out by a girl’s mother or other female relatives—once co-opted into the social equilibrium, they played a key role in perpetuating it. Analogously, college graduates often act to further the PMC’s interests directly via roles in academia, and indirectly via their support for the current education system and the elite political consensus.

Another feature of distributed agency is coordinated behavior to defend the current equilibrium. At one point the Chinese government (specifically the foreign Manchu dynasty) tried to ban foot-binding, but was thwarted by the resistance of the Han Chinese population. To explain this, we need to ascribe the foot-binding equilibrium the ability to generalize to defending itself in novel situations, by mobilizing its adherents towards coordinated action.

Modern educated elites can similarly display a level of collective vitriol that’s hard to explain except as a defense of their class interests. The most obvious example is the PMC’s contempt for blue-collar workers, and for the “Red Tribe” of America more generally—not just its politics, but also its pastimes, culture, and religion. When political movements have arisen that oppose the PMC’s interests—most notably Trump, Brexit, and the “far right” across Europe—cultural elites have mobilized in near-lockstep against them, with very forceful (often to the point of hysterical) rhetoric.

More recently, the PMC has also taken an adversarial stance towards what Scott Alexander calls the “Gray Tribe”, an outgrowth of the Blue Tribe which has formed a distinct power structure over the last few decades, and is therefore being treated as a defector by the Blue Tribe. For example, mainstream journalists adopted an across-the-board hostility to Silicon Valley (and especially to initiatives like the Thiel fellowship which offered an alternative to higher education). Meanwhile, academics often dismiss intellectual progress presented in non-standard ways. The example of this that I’ve observed most directly is the ML community’s failure to engage seriously with the concept of AGI risk (as I discuss in more detail here). Caplan and his colleagues in the GMU economics department themselves provide another example. They demonstrate that professors can be far more intellectually productive when they refuse to submit to standard academic norms—and, relatedly, have faced widespread criticism.

When we encounter any given example of such a response, it’s tempting to ascribe it to an individual’s personal values. But the uniformity of these responses is a strong indicator that they’re instead tracking, and being guided by, a kind of class-wide consensus. However, I don’t mean to imply that the PMC is thereby actually furthering its class interests. As the enormous backlash of the last decade suggests, this level of hostility towards its rivals seems like “irrational” behavior from the PMC. More specifically, it seems like the kind of groupthink-driven overreach that consenses of power are prone to. Unfortunately, the Gray Tribe doesn’t understand what’s going on well enough to avoid reimplementing these harmful dynamics themselves. For example, the main purpose of yCombinator now seems to be forming a similar kind of alumni community as top universities do. (Meanwhile, the AI safety community made the opposite mistake of not gatekeeping enough, which led to the breakdown of alignment research as a meaningful concept.)

Although this post has discussed distributed agents in an informal fashion, much of my research aims to develop a formal theory of distributed agency as rigorous as other leading theories of intelligent agency. This will require progress in game theory and epistemology. Ultimately, I hope that it will ground out in a theory analogous to microeconomics or evolution via natural selection, which describe the emergence of complex structure from multi-agent interactions. However, this post has tried to demonstrate how, even in the absence of the full theory, these ideas can help a lot in understanding the shape of the modern world.

Thanks to Michael Vassar, Ben Landau-Taylor and Hazard Spence for conversations which inspired many of these ideas.

item.title: The Last Interview
item.description:
I arrive at the building at 8:55 in a scheduled Waymo. AIs run this place and I’m still not sure what exactly the company does, but they’re offering paid work and that’s what I need. A robot greets me at the door and tells me to have a seat—in fact, there is only one seat—and then moves to stand near the solitary inner door. Is it welcoming me or guarding against me? Likely both, but it’s not like there’s anywhere for the robot to sit. No need for a reception desk when everything you’d put on a desk is inside the receptionist.

At exactly 9:00am I’m called into the interview room by a speaker in the tiled ceiling. The interview room is empty of everything but a seat and a large table. Naively, I had still expected an interviewer. The table though, is replete with household items of all sorts, including a laptop PC in the centre with the screen glowing towards me.

Another speaker in the ceiling welcomes me briefly and confirms my name and a few details on my resume. Why the two year gap since my last employment? Well, I was a computer programmer, and it’s been hard to find anything… The speaker seems to understand.

“Draw a pelican riding a bicycle.”

I know this one. I’ve even practised for something like it. I sit on the office chair and wheel it in to use the laptop. They’ve got Adobe Illustrator installed but I’ve heard that’s a trick they try to catch you on—basically cheating. I open VSCode and start writing the SVG by hand.

“Please use the art supplies.”

Oh. OH. Right. These guys are already good at computer use. It’ll be human skills they need. Shit. I take a pencil and paper and try to draw a pelican on a bicycle but I’ll be damned if I can remember what a bicycle frame actually looks like. And the proportions of a pelican just don’t work for this; his legs are too short. I’ve messed it up and I can’t make them reach the pedals. In a panic I give him little wooden stilts to bridge the gap.

There’s a whirring sound which I can only imagine is a camera refocusing. Yep, there it is on the ceiling, zooming in.

They let me go home after that, which seems like a bad sign. Just as I’m walking out the door I get an email stating that they don’t wish to go any further with me but I'm welcome to apply again any time. It’s all very polite. They even give me a little feedback, that my pelican wasn’t up to standard with the best candidates but they liked the creativity of the stilts. That part was a mistake…

I go back and carefully reread the job description. It’s light on details but it says they need people with “human skills” and I think I know what they mean. I go home and practise art. I practise sculpture. I build myself a wooden chair. I try to think about all the important and subtle and unique qualities of human life.

Two months later I try again.

“Write a poem using the fridge magnets.”

They’ve even given me a damn fridge. Luckily I’ve studied poetry now, a little. It’s hard to work with the limited vocabulary but in some ways the constraints make it easier somehow as well. I try to capture something unique about the human experience. I can tell that’s what they want, now.

It takes me a good thirty minutes but in the end I’m actually pretty happy with what I’ve got. I must have used more than half of the available words.

But again they send me right home.

Well, I need a job more than ever now, and this is pretty much the only thing going. I study more. I try to think of anything a human might do that an AI can’t. But they’re good at writing now. They’re good at music. They’re good at art. They’re good at poetry.

A few weeks later I decide to just go back. I don’t think I’ll ever be that much more ready than I am now, and they don’t seem to care if I keep applying. Probably takes almost no real effort for them to do an interview.

“Write a short story about your childhood.”

I think about my childhood. I think about how it used to be possible to really be the best at something. I think about how I used to enjoy writing code, solving the puzzle of it. I remember when we were allowed to drive a car ourselves.

Instead of writing a story about my childhood I write “FUCK YOU.” I’m not sure where to go after that so I just write “FUCK YOU” about a fifty more times. They end the interview again after that, but on the way out I get the acceptance email.

item.title: Do general-purpose robots meaningfully increase ASI takeover risk?
item.description:
Recently, I’ve been thinking about the implications of a world where general-purpose robots are developed before AGI. (In such a world, I imagine, trillions of robots would permeate society, replace factory workers, work in homes, etc.)

One implication could be increased AI takeover risk. Intuitively, widespread robots might make takeover substantially easier for a variety of reasons, such as by giving a ASI readily available physical actors and making it easier to secure datacenters / other physical infrastructure crucial to AI. On the other hand, a superintelligence may have an unfathomable number of other ways to gain power or cause extinction. If takeover is thus already likely through other routes, perhaps pre-existing robots add only a negligible amount to total risk.

TLDR: Does anyone know of good discussions on whether widespread general-purpose robots before ASI would meaningfully increase takeover risk?

I’ve found scarcely anything on this; discussions from Paul Christiano and Nick Bostrom, for instance, argue that AI could take over without general-purpose robots, but don’t address how much additional risk pre-existing general-purpose robots would create.

If anyone knows of relevant readings or discussions, would really appreciate it. Also, I understand the effect is difficult to quantify, so am just trying to get a sense of how people think about its likely magnitude.

item.title: Abstraction Equivocation
item.description:
During my outreach, onboarding, and lobbying for PauseAI, there’s a pattern of mistaken reasoning I see repeatedly, which I expect to become higher stakes with Senators Sanders and Casar’s recent proposal to ban superintelligence.  I’m going to call it Abstraction Equivocation, which is applying implementation or trust level critiques to directional proposals.

Here’s what I mean by these terms:

Directional: about priorities, goals, and central assumptions.  As examples of priorities: preventing x-risk from AI is non-negotiable and required for anything else to matter; competitiveness is a constraint other values need to work within to not undercut themselves; equity, innovation, and stability trade off with each other in context-dependent ways, with room for legitimate disagreement as to the proper balance.  As examples of central assumptions: superintelligent AI is a meaningful concept, likely to occur in a relevant timeframe, and extremely dangerous if not handled well.  Directional critiques should engage with whether these are the right priorities and if their foundational assumptions make sense.

Implementation: about specific mechanisms.  Does a given definition of superintelligence capture what is intended, exclude what is not, and is there a clear way to tell?  Will a given monitoring system catch what it needs to catch?  Such questions require a clear point of reference.

Trust: about who decides the details.  Can a given agency be trusted to make good decisions without getting captured?  Can the courts be trusted to interpret key definitions correctly?  Trust sits at the bridge between direction and implementation, applying to proposals that are directional, but with a plan to fill in the details, assessing the people who are responsible for that filling in.

These levels are relative and recursive.  International coordination, for example, is directional relative to the monitoring and enforcement regimes applied, and also an implementation of preventing x-risk.  High level proposals for monitoring, in turn, are implementation details of coordination, and also directional in the sense that they need to be implemented on a technical level--at the direction of specific agencies, which require trust.

Here are some common examples of what I consider Abstraction Equivocation:

The US can’t slow down AI development or else China will race ahead

Assumes that a hypothetical agreement will not contain adequate monitoring and enforcement provisions to prevent exactly this from happening.  You have to actually look at the relevant provisions to know if they are inadequate.

Regulating AI will lock-in a monopoly for industry incumbents

Assumes that hypothetical regulation will introduce extensive bureaucratic red tape that applies equally to everyone, creating a high-cost barrier to entry.  In reality, actual proposals where this objection tends to be raised (1) focus on frontier development, which is vastly more gated by compute and infrastructure costs, such that regulation is a drop in the bucket, and (2) have cost thresholds below which the regulation does not apply--and sometimes even specific carveouts for open source.

Or to put it in simpler terms: RTFB or GTFO.

In contrast, here are some example objections that are based on the same worldviews as the above, but don’t involve Abstraction Equivocation:

Directional: Concerns about “x-risk” are overblown.  AI alignment, to the extent it was ever a meaningful concept, is basically solved.  We should prioritize innovation so that we get the benefits of AI as soon as possible.

Implementation: “Superintelligence” is poorly defined in this bill and could be reasonably interpreted to include all sorts of normal technologies.

Trust: Once you create any sort of government agency to regulate AI, it’s going to be subject to perverse incentives to drift from its original purpose and centralize power in the national government or create regulatory moats for industry incumbents.

These examples vary widely in how wrong I believe they are, but each at least clearly points toward what kind of response it invites.

Spotting Abstraction Equivocation in the wild can be tricky, because directional-sounding statements can imply expectations about implementation.  Consider this recent X post from Dwarkesh Patel (which I'm picking on because it's subtle not because it's egregious):

Notice that it never actually quotes, paraphrases, or summarizes any provisions in any particular piece of legislation (such as the Sanders-Casar bill) that are inadequate, underspecified, or likely to lead to unintended consequences.  For example, the argument that: “During a pause of AI development, compute would continue to build up” assumes that the bill doesn’t contain adequate compute tracking and governance.  Maybe it doesn’t.  Maybe its attempts are underspecified.  Maybe the details have been delegated to an agency that lacks sufficient authority, competence, or trustworthiness.  All of these are different objections, requiring different responses, and I don’t know which one Dwarkesh is making.

This example is especially pointed given the clear context of a bill to cite.  But even if Dwarkesh was narrowly responding to Sanders' directional call for a ban on superintelligence, the same issue of Abstraction Equivocation applies. The implied structure is: “Any proposal of type X must contain features A, B, and C, feature B has consequences D, E, and F, consequence F is really bad, therefore X is bad.”  But all that gets said out loud is: “X is bad because F.”

Directional, implementation, and trust objections all have their place.  Directional disagreements cut to our core values, engaging on a philosophical level about how to manage tradeoffs between different things that matter, and set the stage for what categories of policy even make sense to consider.  Their universality makes directional proposals accessible to everyone, which is why PauseAI’s proposals have often been of this type.  But at some point, philosophy needs to cache out into policy, and that requires details to get right.  This is where implementation objections come in, red-teaming the details of how grand ideas get put into practice, anticipating and avoiding unintended consequences.  When dealing with complex, evolving issues, however, such details can’t be planned out in advance, but must rather be delegated to entities with a defined scope of authority.  At that point, it becomes essential to ask whether those entities are trustworthy.

What doesn't help is conflating these types.  A bad goal can’t be fixed by achieving it better; good intentions can’t fix poor implementation.  Getting the category right determines whether a conversation can make progress.

In improv, 'yes, and' accepts the premise of a scene and builds on it.  “Yes, but” accepts it and redirects, or adds a conflict to overcome.  A “no” blocks the scene from happening, forcing others to find a way to start over.  In the real world, our goal is to move towards good futures, not dramatic ones, so sufficiently directional disagreement is a legitimate reason to say “no.”  But such obstruction should label itself clearly, not disguise itself as engagement.

item.title: A Therapist for People Who Think the World Might End: An Interview with Daystar Eld (Damon Sasi)
item.description:
I sat down with therapist and writer Damon Sasi, better known online as Daystar Eld, for one of the conversations I’ve found myself referencing most often since recording it.

We talk about what’s bullshit and what isn’t in therapy, therapy for rationalists, and how to stay psychologically healthy when you genuinely believe the end of the world may be coming.

We also cover executive function, whether therapists are sometimes substitutes for friendships, and what actually helps people change. We talk about rationality and effective altruism, dating, and the modern dating crisis.

We spend a lot of time on AI companions, AI girlfriends and boyfriends, wireheading, chatbot psychosis, and what happens when artificial partners can be tailored to us more perfectly than another human being ever could.

And of course we discuss rationalist fiction, Pokémon, the influence of Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality, and his magnum opus: Pokémon: The Origin of Species!

Please enjoy the interview! (Timestamps and transcript below.)

Transcript

(Note: This is transcribed with AI and some parts are corrected by hand but I haven't gone through the entire transcript so there are most certainly errors!)

John: Okay, could you say your name, your background and what you're currently working on?

Damon: Sure. My name is Damon Pourtahmaseb-Sasi. I usually just go by Damon Sasi. I also am known as Daystar Eld online, my website and my handle on most websites is Daystar Eld. I'm a therapist by default, I've been doing a lot of fiction writing for over 25 years. I've written novels, I've written nonfiction articles on psych research and just various different blogging topics about like psychology and mental health and social stuff. I teach at various camps and workshops around the world. I've led a few of them myself. I run WARP, the Wandering Applied Rationality Program, for 2023, 2024, and 2025. These days I'm mostly just doing some therapy, doing some writing and working on the next ideas for workshops that I want to have.

John: You're one of these people we have to hate that's so accomplished and has so many things going on that it's like, how do you have the time and energy?

Damon: That's the trick. You don't. You procrastinate sometimes and you let things fall through the cracks and like you end up doing only like half the things you really want to do. And then, yeah.

John: So do you think it's that the things that you actually want to do will just sort of rise to the surface?

Damon: Yeah. I, so obviously I've written a lot about Procedural Executive Function, which is my name a way to understand it. So I've written a lot about Procedural Executive Function, which is my name a way to understand executive function in a way that helps people isolate, like what's actually works for them and what isn't and like where they're stuck when they're stuck doing any particular thing they want to do. One of the major things I try to highlight is that your experience of motivation is always going to be driven by what you really want to do or you really need to do. And the need thing is kind of wonky in the modern Western world because we did not evolve for most of the shit we are that tell us we need to do things that our limbic system has not evolved to understand as an individual. Like a need which is a lot of what I think a lot of executive dysfunction comes down to, because this function comes down to but the one thing is pretty important. There are some people who get lucky in some ways. And one of the ways they get lucky is like the thing they really are driven to do happens to be a thing that they are good at and people will reward them for. And I am lucky in some senses. And one of the ways that I'm lucky is that like, I got really into psychology and therapy. I seem to be pretty good at it. It's a job that people seem willing to and happy to pay me for. I am really into writing. I seem to be good. It's something that people are willing to pay me for. And I turned out to be a pretty good teacher and I enjoy it. And people are willing to invite me to things to teach stuff. If one of my major interests had turned out to be stamp collecting or something like I probably would enjoy that and find it very enriching my life, but I would not I would not be as accomplished. It's like it's like one of those kinds of things.

John: Yeah. Where did you grow up?

Damon: Miami. I was born and raised in Miami. I lived there for 30 years. And that's basically traveling at all that much elsewhere like family trips once a while or something like that. But after COVID is where I started traveling a lot more. And I started teaching where I started teaching at the camps, and workshops and stuff. I would travel more for like during the summers.

John: Yeah. Were you in Coral Gables, or...?

Damon: Miami. No actual Miami. Miami-Dade county area, like near Aventura. People know what that is, but not Aventura itself. 'Cause that's very rich.

John: Yeah. I lived in Boca for four years. Yeah. Really familiar. How did you get tapped into this community?

Damon: Yeah. I found HPMOR like many people just kind of randomly, which was weird for me because I hadn't read any fan fiction up until that point. I had written fan fiction, but I never read any. And I can't even remember what subreddit I found it on, but I found HPMOR and I read it and I was like, this is amazing. I had never read something like this, and I wanted to read more things like this back then. They were like, this was back in like 2011 or something. So there wasn't much rational fiction out there. So I read what there was, which was, I think, only Luminosity, The Metropolitan Man, maybe one other thing that I'm forgetting. And I read those and I was like, this is cool. I want more of this to exist. I'm going to write more of this. And yeah, I met Alexander Wales after reading more of his stories, like his short stories that were rational. It's also Branches on the Tree of Time and stuff. And I started writing Pokémon: The Origin of Species. And I just spent four years being a therapist in Miami, writing Pokémon fan fiction. And then at some point in 2017. Yeah. I was emailed by someone who was like, Hey, I've been reading your fiction. You seem pretty good at teaching this stuff in your fiction. Do you want to come teach at these camps? And I'm like, that sounds cool. What are you talking about? I'm like, this is this thing called CFAR. And then you can go to CFAR. If you go to CFAR, then you can come teach at ESPR. I was like, okay, sure. I'll try that out.

John: It's a, I think HPMOR was like, the gateway drug for so many people to get into, but you were already into fan fiction. You didn't read it. You just wrote it.

Damon: Yeah. I want to say. I wrote it. What I mean is that like, I wrote a lot of stuff, some of them original fiction, some of them not original fiction. And then like occasionally the, some of the stuff I would write would be fan fiction. I don't think I posted any fan fiction on the internet until that point. I think I mostly just wrote it for my own.

John: I see.

Damon: But when I found the fan fiction, the rational fiction community, and we kind of created a rational fiction community out of the HPMOR community on Reddit. We created a new subreddit for it and Discord and everything. It was very much like, oh, this is, oh, intersection of two of my special interests, like understanding psychology and people better and understanding myself better and like fiction. And I just kind of stopped writing all the other stuff that I was writing at the time. That wasn't rational fiction. I had a book that I'd finished that I was like looking at editors for to get published. And I just didn't want to publish it anymore after I read HPMOR because I was just like, this isn't good enough, so I abandoned it.

John: Yeah. Can you explain what rationalist fiction is? Cool. We have trouble with definitions here.

Damon: Rational. It's a rationalist itself. It itself. There's like a, as like a word that's loaded aspiring rationalist is probably a better word for people who like, don't believe that they're perfectly rational, but want to be more rational. Rational fiction is like, roughly speaking, any fiction that is trying really hard to be consistent in the way the rules of the world work out in which the characters themselves are trying to be consistent with their motivations. It's not saying that they always pick the perfect option. It's like, if they make a mistake, it's a mistake that makes sense given their emotional makeup and their incentives and their history. And not just the plot clearly demanded that they knew that it's not just that the writer really wanted this outcome to happen. So they just wrote that outcome. We'll go with whether it made sense for the character to do it. I think pretty popular, not spoilery at this point. Example, if you watched Game of Thrones and you got to the last few seasons and you're like, what the fuck are they doing? Like rational fiction tries not to do that. It's like you can put extra effort into your fiction to make it more legible to the reader and more predictable to the reader in a way that doesn't rob it of its emotional power and its like surprises and all this kind of stuff. I think there's some authors out there that like people might think are rational authors, even if they don't use that title. And I think some of those are, and some of them aren't, I think like Brandon Sanderson is an example that people tend to bring up as like, oh, but his magic systems are really like rigid and understandable and like and like well thought out. And I would agree with that, except in my opinion, Brandon Sanderson cheats. Like he will explicitly have his characters pull some random magic out of their ass at the last minute to save the day. And that is a thing that rational fiction tries really hard not to do. And so rational fiction just tries to do that too. It tries to make that like ideal more of the thing that they do. And then rationalist fiction is like when the protagonists are themselves explicitly or implicitly like thinking in a rationalist way such that you can like learn good epistemics from them. Usually using things that like we would recognize as part of like the community's ideas of what good rational thinking is, like Bayesian. Map versus territory distinctions or like trying to, yeah, just trying to falsify their hypotheses in interesting and agentic ways that yeah.

John: I think a lot of it is it makes it more enjoyable, even though it's harder because it's like when you're watching a horror movie and then you're going, yeah, who would do this? No one would do that. It doesn't make any sense. And so you're not having that voice constantly screaming.

Damon: Hopefully. Yeah. If it's done. And I mean, I'm definitely like, I've written Pokémon now for over 12 years, up until recently, one chapter a month, every month, come whatever happened in life, which sometimes is a lot. And I would try to spend that month putting in as much effort as I could, researching everything I could to make it good. And I would still, I mean, I, at some point I eventually had many, many readers. And at some point, some readers would be like, what about this thing? Fuck, I forgot about that thing. It's like, it's not, you can't. It can't be perfect. It's not, the goal is not to be perfect. It's just trying really hard to actually make it. Yeah. Trying.

John: Yeah. Were you just really into the games when you were younger or how did you...

Damon: Oh yeah. So when I picked Pokémon, in part because they were like, basically I had like three major ideas for what I would write. One of them was, there's this story called Dealing with Dragons. My online handle, the first half of it comes from the fourth of these, Talking to Dragons, the protagonist's name is Daystar. I saw it like it was a really great series. When I was young, it was a kind of like deconstructing fantasy tropes, which is similar to rational fiction in some way. And I enjoyed it a lot. And I thought of writing that, and I thought of writing an Animorphs rational fic, 'cause I really like Animorphs. I'm glad that I didn't, 'cause Duncan Sabien has since written a rationalist Animorphs fiction. That's way better than the one I would have written. And then Pokémon was the other one I thought of because I loved Pokémon when I was young, like spent many years thinking about it in the world and all the ways it didn't make sense and how to make it more, make more sense. And so it was just like a very clear sense of like, oh yeah, I can. I can write this. I can do as well.

John: Were you playing on your Game Boy Color?

Damon: Yeah, I played the original. I mean, I was a perfect age for Pokémon and Harry Potter. I turned 11 the same year Pokémon came to the United States and the same year Harry Potter was released in the United States. So I grew up with it.

John: Yeah. Were you playing like Red or Blue?

Damon: I played Red and then I played Gold and then I played, I think I played Yellow. So I played Gold and Yellow. I played all the way through till Ruby and then Emerald, and then they remade FireRed and LeafGreen. I played through that. And I was like, yeah. I was like, okay, I think I'm done now. This is like, come back full circle at the time. It came back full circle to the first generation. It was fun. I stopped playing the Pokémon games after that, up until X and Y came out, which was like a few generations later. Yeah. And largely because I started writing Pokémon. And I was like, well, let's see what the games are like nowadays.

John: Yeah. Which starter did you pick in Pokémon Red? Bulbasaur?

Damon: Yeah. I'm a Bulbasaur fan.

John: Nice. Yeah. Too many people are Charmander. Bulbasaur was where it's at. What is your favorite Pokémon?

Damon: Mew is probably my favorite, if not Bulbasaur.

John: Yeah. Mew's pretty good. Did you see the movie and get the Ancient Mew card?

Damon: I did.

John: I saw someone walking around here with Ancient Mew shorts. It was like the same with that design. And I told him, I thought his shorts were pretty cool.

Damon: Yeah. I was super diehard into Pokémon when I was young for many, many years.

John: Did you do the cards?

Damon: Yeah. I have a binder still full of the original.

John: You didn't sell out during COVID.

Damon: I didn't sell out during COVID, although probably I should sell them sooner or later.

John: Yeah. I don't know. A part of me is glad that I don't collect things like that anymore because it's so expensive.

Damon: Yeah. For sure. But I do see the appeal. Yeah. I used to be really into Magic: The Gathering too. And I gave all my Magic: The Gathering cards to my brother a few years, not a few years now, like 10 years ago now. Cause I just don't have time or money to spend on it anymore. But the Pokémon cards I kept for nostalgia and like sentimentality.

John: Yeah. Do you think you'll, do you see an end point to like, you've been so consistent with Pokémon: The Origin of Species, do you see, oh, I could end it, or would it feel like...

Damon: No, yeah, I had an ending in mind when I started, I had a specific vague, it was somewhat vague, but still fairly solid idea of where it would be going. So my idea was basically like going from the start that I had envisioned, get it from one bright spot to the next, till it reaches the end, kind of filling in along the way as I go. And that ending has more or less stayed the same since the beginning. And a lot has changed in the middle, but the ending is more or less stayed the same. I thought, I think I can finish the story in another roughly 20 chapters. But like two more years, roughly. That's what I thought. As I kind of mentioned earlier, unfortunately, my dad's been going through some health issues lately. And it's been kind of hard to write along with some other things. I've also had things going on in my life alongside that for the past half a year or so. So it's been, I've been trying to kind of write when I can, and thankfully my readers have been very understanding. I feel like I'm slowly spending down 11 years of goodwill of being so consistent with my fiction. They're like, okay, this is, we'll accept this, but yeah, I really want to finish it. I've written a lot of other stuff in the meantime that people have asked me, why aren't you writing this? You can get this published. Even this is original fiction. They're like, yeah, that's true. I'm going to go back to writing Pokémon now though. So yeah, I wanted to finish.

John: Yeah. You don't want to be like George R. R. Martin.

Damon: Yeah. I'll be honest at this point. I mean, the AI is nowhere near good enough to write good fiction in my opinion, but like at this point, if AI gets better and I can just give it the entire book and then my own notes or something, and it produces the rest of the story. And I have the opportunity to like edit it and be like, Hmm, like good here. No, that's not right. And then go through that. I would probably just do that. I don't feel at this point, I don't feel like, no, I need to be the one that finishes it. If some person in particular was like, Hey, I have an idea for how, like the story would end and here I'm going to write my version of the ending. And it was really good. I'd be like, that's good. I'm happy to go with that because there are many other things I'd like to do and like things I'd like to write and things that are on my mind and stuff. And 12 years is a long time to be on one project. I think. Yeah.

John: I think it shows how little ego you have in it because most people are control freaks and they want to get attached and they're like, this is my thing, forget whatever you're doing.

Damon: Yeah. I guess I've almost always been, I mean, I do enjoy writing. Thankfully. It's kind of go back to the thing I said, where like, it's like lucky that I enjoy writing given everything. But I also just like write stories that I can't find elsewhere that I want to exist. And so if someone else can write it, I have other ideas.

John: Yeah. Wow. You talk about maybe 20 chapters left. We're in the center of the rationality community at Lighthaven. How do you feel about some of the problems that people bring up with worrying about existential risk with AI?

Damon: Yeah. I am psychologically unusual in a number of ways. One of those ways that I'm psychologically unusual is that I seem to be pretty good at not stressing about things outside of my control. Yeah, I see the way other people live and I'm like, man, that sounds, that seems like it sucks. I'm sorry about that. No, there are ways in which I, obviously I'm worried about certain things. That I try to do something about, and there are ways that I try to like double check my own sense of like what I can do and can't do. So I'm not tricking myself into thinking there's nothing I can do about it. Every few years I like actually just like kind of explicitly like think, okay, from first principles now, like what else, what should I be doing with my life that can probably be doing better for the world or for myself or for other people or something like that? Which has been pretty good as a heuristic and it's helped me to make a lot of major changes in life that have continued to pay off very well. But yeah, when it comes to like alignment stuff, I am pretty on board with the fear that like, we are not prepared for AI. I think it is like on a, on an intellectual level, it just seems very clear to me that we are not prepared for the political aspects of it, for the technical aspects of it, for the economic aspects of it, for the military implications of it. And also we are just not prepared for the fundamental idea of like, what does it mean to have an artificial intelligence that is... Smart as us would be a problem. But like something clearly smarter than us I have not heard, I've looked into many of the counter arguments and perspectives of people who are not as worried and mostly they just seem to be really, really high on copium. It's like kind of surprising to me how many otherwise smart and like smart and clever people who I respect seem to be of the belief of like, oh, we'll just figure it out. Like fundamentally, like obviously they wouldn't put it that way, but they seem to be like, yeah, well that's a hard problem. I put like 20% or 30% of it being a big deal and we'll figure it out as we go. And I'm like, yeah, maybe, I don't know. It is, I mean, that's still better than the people who are just like, oh yeah, it's just totally fine or whatever. I think it is a big problem. I hope that we figure it out or figure out what to do about it. I would like to find more ways to help if I can. Right now it's been hard for me to notice any of like obvious things to do. I've talked to a few people about it and some people have suggested some potentially interesting ideas that I should probably look into more.

John: But you have a lot on your plate.

Damon: Yeah. Well, I don't know, like yes and no, like there's a lot on my plate, but if, I don't know if someone genuinely was like, Hey, this would be really helpful to us to figure out this particular problem. I'd probably be like, Hey guys, sorry, but I should probably put Pokémon on hold to figure this out or something.

John: Right. Yeah. Your fans would be like, fuck it. Let's get it launched. And then, yeah. But 20 months, depending on your timelines.

Damon: Yeah. I mean, so, okay. So the timelines thing goes back to the weird psychology thing. Intellectually, I think this all makes sense to me emotionally. Like I, it doesn't really matter to me that much, whether it's like five years, 20 years or a hundred years for like as far as I can see, we do not have a plan for aligning AI. And that is going to be a problem for our children or grandchildren. If it's not a problem for us, if it is a problem for us, maybe it is going to be only a few years. I'm not a technical person. Like my models of like how AI, if it, even if it becomes super intelligent would manage to end the world without us being able to do anything about it, are not completely solid or something. I kind of, I'm just like kind of borrowing knowledge in some sense, which may be why emotionally it doesn't feel like as alive to me that like, oh, we might all be dead in two years or something like, yeah, maybe. But to me, the problem still needs to be solved. Regardless. And my life is, I feel like I went through the grief process of like, okay. Like maybe I will not live to like have children or something or finish my work that I care about, but that was still true even before the AI thing. And it is worse. It was definitely worse than the whole world might end instead of just my life. But yeah.

John: A lot of people in the community suffer from mental health issues because they're so worried about doom. What advice do you give them?

Damon: Well, first I'd want to distinguish like is the doom causal or just feeding into something that's already there? I mean, I think it's true that for some people it is feeding into something that's already there. I think some people it is causal. I think there's a lot of things like there's a couple of really good articles written by Gretta Duleba and Duncan Sabien. The titles, I think, are something like A Way to Be Okay, Another Way to Be Okay. Pull them up to check to make sure. Oh, A Way to Be Okay. I think that's what it's called, actually. A Way to Be Okay. And Another Way to Be Okay. Yeah. On LessWrong. I think these are like basically coming down to some mix though. The thing I said about noticing what's in your control and what's not grieving process is important. Grief is not just for when people die. It's also for like in preparation for things that might happen or will happen. Accepting. So like heroic responsibility is this really cool concept I think in the rationality community and the EA community is this idea that like you should try to act as though there's no one who's going to save you, who's going to do the thing that you think needs to happen, who's going to make sure things go well. Like how would you act if you knew that you were actually the person responsible for making sure things go well? And I would say that heroic responsibility is really, really good in a way as a way to orient towards your life and like how a way to orient to like how to make things in your environment better. And as it starts to go outward from that and starts to affect like the world itself, it's really important to be able to like put that lens on to like figure out what's the best thing is. But burnout is a thing that happens. I think not just from like this concept of overwork, it comes from having a mismatch of responsibility and power. I've written about this on my blog. It's like, I think most of the time when you look at someone who burns out, it's because, either because of their internal drive or their bosses or something, they have so much responsibility that they do not have enough power to affect.
